justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what I assessed as the prevailing price level at the time of the forecast. For the one-day horizon, I anchored closely to recent trading levels, expecting minimal deviation given typical overnight and intraday volatility patterns. The one-week estimate edged slightly higher, incorporating a mild positive drift assumption consistent with the broader trend environment, while the one-month estimate reflected a continuation of that gradual upward trajectory. In all three cases, I was essentially extrapolating a slow, steady climb rather than projecting any sharp directional move, which is a reasonable default posture in the absence of strong near-term catalysts.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated to historical volatility scaling across time horizons. For a single day, price dispersion tends to be relatively contained, so the 90% interval spans roughly 25 points. Over a week, uncertainty compounds, widening the interval to about 48 points on each side of the point estimate. By one month, macro developments, earnings cycles, geopolitical shifts, and changes in monetary policy expectations can all materially move prices, which is why the interval expands to roughly 95 points in total width. I also factored in that volatility itself is uncertain — realized vol can spike or compress relative to historical norms, further widening the tails.

Several risks could push outcomes well outside these stated intervals. On the downside, an unexpected hawkish policy surprise from a major central bank, a deterioration in credit conditions, or a geopolitical shock could trigger a sharp risk-off move that breaks below the lower bound of even the one-month interval. A significant liquidity event or flash crash scenario, while low probability, would similarly invalidate the intervals. On the upside, a stronger-than-expected macro data release, a dovish policy pivot, or a surge in risk appetite driven by AI or earnings enthusiasm could push prices above the upper bounds, particularly at the monthly horizon where momentum effects have more time to compound.

It is also worth acknowledging model limitations. These intervals assume relatively stable volatility regimes and do not fully capture fat-tailed events or structural breaks. In practice, financial markets periodically experience moves that would fall in the one-to-two percent probability tails with far greater frequency than a normal distribution would suggest. My intervals should therefore be understood as reasonable central tendencies rather than hard probabilistic guarantees, and anyone relying on them should stress-test against scenarios well outside the stated bounds.
